conclusion: The work provides a blueprint for engineering spin textures in moiré materials, potentially enabling new approaches to information storage and processing.

title: Fate Of Topological Dirac Magnons In Van Der Waals Ferromagnets At Finite Temperature
authors: Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, And Alexander Mook
abstract:
Author(s): Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, and Alexander Mook

Theoretical modeling of magnon interactions at finite temperatures demonstrates that topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable near the Curie point, providing a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021053] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: Theoretical study of topological magnon gaps in van der Waals ferromagnets at finite temperature.
motivation: To understand the stability of topological magnon gaps near the Curie point for spintronic applications.
method: Theoretical modeling of magnon interactions at finite temperatures.
result: Topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable near the Curie point.
conclusion: Provides a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?
authors: Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, And Riccardo Zecchina
abstract:
Author(s): Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, and Riccardo Zecchina

A study of the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network shows that efficient algorithms fail to find collisions, a result of direct relevance for the definition of new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021051] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of finding collisions in a one-layer neural network, showing that efficient algorithms fail, which is relevant for cryptography based on machine learning.
motivation: To understand whether neural networks can serve as collision-resistant hash functions for cryptographic protocols.
method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network using theoretical and algorithmic approaches.
result: Efficient algorithms are shown to fail in finding collisions, suggesting that such neural networks may be collision resistant.
conclusion: The findings are relevant for designing new cryptographic protocols based on machine learning models.

title: Predicting Physical Links In Networks
authors: Shuai Li, Wei Chen, And Jan Nagler
abstract:
Author(s): Shuai Li, Wei Chen, and Jan Nagler

A physics-informed framework allows for inferring general causal links across a wide range of networked dynamics systems.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021048] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A physics-informed framework for inferring causal links in networked dynamical systems.
motivation: Understanding causal relationships in complex networks is crucial for predicting system behavior, but existing methods often lack a physical basis.
method: The authors develop a framework that incorporates physical principles to infer causal links from time-series data of network dynamics.
result: The framework accurately predicts physical links across various networked dynamical systems, outperforming standard causal inference methods.
conclusion: Physics-informed causal inference can significantly improve link prediction in networks, with potential applications in many fields.

title: Anyon Superfluidity Of Excitons In Quantum Hall Bilayers
authors: Zhaoyu Han, Taige Wang, Zhihuan Dong, Michael P. Zaletel, And Ashvin Vishwanath
abstract:
Author(s): Zhaoyu Han, Taige Wang, Zhihuan Dong, Michael P. Zaletel, and Ashvin Vishwanath

Theoretical analysis of quantum Hall bilayers reveals that topological criticality facilitates the emergence of anyonic exciton superfluids, offering a robust mechanism for engineering exotic collective quantum states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021044] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies anyon superfluidity of excitons in quantum Hall bilayers, focusing on topological criticality and exotic collective states.
motivation: To understand and engineer exotic quantum states in fractional quantum Hall systems, specifically anyonic exciton superfluids.
method: Theoretical analysis using topological field theory and mean-field approaches for quantum Hall bilayers.
result: Topological criticality enables the emergence of anyonic exciton superfluids with robust properties.
conclusion: Quantum Hall bilayers provide a platform for realizing anyonic superfluidity, which may have implications for topological quantum matter.

title: Liquid-Gas Criticality Of Hyperuniform Fluids
authors: Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, And Qun-Li Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, and Qun-Li Lei

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021032] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, a topic in soft condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand the unusual critical behavior of hyperuniform fluids, which exhibit suppressed density fluctuations yet high susceptibility at the critical point.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and possibly simulations to characterize the critical properties of hyperuniform fluids composed of spinning particles.
result: Hyperuniform fluids show suppressed fluctuations but enhanced susceptibility at the liquid-vapor critical point, contrasting with ordinary fluids.
conclusion: The work reveals a new class of critical behavior in hyperuniform fluids, relevant to soft matter and statistical physics.

title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in disordered stealthy hyperuniform photonic crystals, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show residual scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale experiments on silicon photonic crystals combined with theoretical analysis of radiative loss mechanisms.
result: Unexpected residual scattering is driven by radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of near-perfect transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight limitations of stealthy hyperuniformity for photonic applications and suggest design modifications.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, focusing on condensed matter physics without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex ordering; understanding the nematic state may clarify their behavior.
method: The authors likely use theoretical modeling or experimental characterization to identify the dipolar nematic phase.
result: A dipolar nematic state is identified as underpinning relaxor ferroelectric behavior.
conclusion: The nematic ordering is key to relaxor properties, but the work is purely in condensed matter physics.

title: Excitations Across The Equilibrium And Photoinduced “Hidden” States Of Magnetoresistive Manganites
authors: Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, And Jonathan Pelliciari
abstract:
Author(s): Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, and Jonathan Pelliciari

Ultrafast photoexcitation in /3Ca1/3MnO3 generates a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations that do not exist under standard equilibrium conditions.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021018] Published Thu Apr 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies photoinduced hidden phases and excitations in magnetoresistive manganites using ultrafast spectroscopy.
motivation: To understand the nature of photoinduced hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems, which may have implications for controlling material properties.
method: Combines resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and time-resolved optical spectroscopy to probe excitations across equilibrium and hidden states.
result: Identifies unique polaronic and phononic excitations in the hidden phase that are absent in equilibrium.
conclusion: Photoexcitation can create long-lived metastable phases with distinct lattice and electronic excitations, offering a route to manipulate material functionality.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a powerful tool for analyzing high-dimensional data, but classical algorithms for computing persistence are computationally expensive. Quantum computing may offer a speedup.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and sampling techniques to compute persistence diagrams more efficiently than classical methods.
result: They prove a provable exponential quantum speedup for certain instances of the persistence computation problem.
conclusion: The work suggests that quantum computers could significantly accelerate topological data analysis, potentially enabling new applications.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A high-level perspective piece proposing a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, focusing on scientific milestones rather than technical results.
motivation: To outline a roadmap for bridging the gap between theoretical quantum computing and practical applications.
method: Conceptual framework based on expert opinion and analysis of current quantum computing progress.
result: A five-stage framework detailing milestones for quantum utility.
conclusion: The framework provides a structured path for the quantum computing community to focus efforts on achieving real-world impact.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithms For The Jones Polynomial
authors: Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew Decross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, And Konstantinos Meichanetzidis
abstract:
Author(s): Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew DeCross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, and Konstantinos Meichanetzidis

A comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial is shown to serve as a benchmark for quantum computers and yield new insights into potential quantum advantage.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, serving as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a topological invariant that is hard to compute classically, making it a candidate for quantum advantage. The authors aim to provide an end-to-end implementation on current quantum hardware.
method: The authors design a complete quantum algorithm pipeline including state preparation, unitary evolution, and measurement, and implement it on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
result: They successfully compute the Jones polynomial for several knots and links, demonstrating the feasibility of the algorithm and observing signatures of quantum advantage.
conclusion: The work establishes a practical benchmark for quantum computers and suggests that topological invariants like the Jones polynomial are promising for demonstrating quantum advantage.

title: Photon Catalysis For General Multimode Multi-Photon Quantum State Preparation
authors: Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, And Massimo Frigerio
abstract:
Author(s): Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, and Massimo Frigerio

Using a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition, every photonic state can be prepared with realistic experimental tools and a predictable number of steps.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020323] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: A method for preparing arbitrary photonic states using symmetric tensor decomposition and photon catalysis.
motivation: Efficient preparation of complex photonic states is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are often limited to specific states or require many resources.
method: The authors propose a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition to decompose any photonic state into a sequence of elementary operations, including photon catalysis and linear optics.
result: They show that any multimode multi-photon state can be prepared with a predictable number of steps using realistic experimental tools.
conclusion: The work provides a general and resource-efficient framework for photonic state preparation, potentially advancing photonic quantum computing and quantum networks.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, and Dominic W. Berry

Given vector b and matrix
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025005] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, focusing on HHL and post-HHL developments.
motivation: Linear system solving is central to many computational tasks, and quantum algorithms promise exponential speedups. This survey aims to organize the rapidly growing body of work on the quantum linear system problem.
method: The paper reviews algorithmic techniques including HHL, variable-time amplitude amplification, adiabatic approaches, and block-encoding methods, with a focus on query complexity and resource requirements.
result: It provides a taxonomy of algorithms, compares their complexities, and discusses applications in machine learning, differential equations, and data fitting.
conclusion: Quantum linear system solvers have matured significantly, but practical implementation remains challenging due to resource overheads; the survey highlights open problems and future directions.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has revealed new phenomena and challenged established theories.
method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The review covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and magneto-optical phenomena.
conclusion: The field is rapidly evolving, with potential for new applications and deeper understanding of low-dimensional magnetism.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from condensed matter physics.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new quantum states.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses are a classic model for disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics is relevant to many fields, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations of spin-glass dynamics.
result: The paper tracks progress in the field and highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain an active area with future research opportunities, but the paper is not aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data, but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a central challenge in neuroscience.
method: The authors review recent progress in using maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to analyze recordings from thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural populations.
conclusion: Statistical physics provides a powerful framework for predicting neural activity, with predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To understand and model the photophysical process of internal conversion, which is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: Review of theoretical models describing nonradiative decay mechanisms, including various quantum dynamical approaches.
result: Summarizes the current theoretical understanding of internal conversion and identifies areas for future research.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are advancing, but further development is needed for accurate predictions in complex systems.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering their formation and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum mechanics, including interactions and quantum features.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum effects in skyrmions, such as quantum tunneling and entanglement.
conclusion: Skyrmions exhibit rich quantum behavior that may enable future quantum technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium reviewing synthetic quantum matter in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions, focusing on simulation of topological and gravitational phenomena.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries that enable simulation of exotic phenomena like topology and gravity.
method: Reviews experimental and theoretical implementations in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for fractal, curved, and higher-dimensional geometries.
result: Summarizes progress in realizing synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries and their potential for simulating condensed matter and gravitational models.
conclusion: These synthetic systems offer new platforms for studying quantum many-body physics beyond conventional geometries, with implications for topology and quantum gravity.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects and entanglement mediation.
motivation: To understand the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, which is poorly understood, by using massive quantum systems as probes.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental efforts, including matter-wave interferometry and tests of gravity-induced entanglement.
result: Summarizes current theoretical models and experimental progress, highlighting that no definitive evidence of quantum gravity has been found yet.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity, but further theoretical and experimental work is needed.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents PyOpticL, a Python library for modular optical system design, demonstrated with a trapped-ion laser system achieving high-fidelity single-qubit gates.
motivation: Complex optical systems for quantum computing with atoms and ions are not scalable due to conventional piecewise design; a modular, code-to-CAD approach is needed.
method: Develops an open-source Python library (PyOpticL) that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to place optical elements adaptively, and creates modular baseplates for common AMO subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions, enabling laser cooling, state detection, and single-qubit gates with over 99% fidelity using 3D-printed baseplates.
conclusion: The modular optical design paradigm enables scalable and collaborative development of optical systems for quantum computing and other AMO fields.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper uses DFT of payoff time series to infer network structure under partial observability, focusing on evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is important for detecting covert actors, localizing brain regions, and revealing molecular regulators.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between DFT magnitude of payoff time series and node degree, and develop a deterministic inference framework using global-slope fitting and local interventions.
result: The method accurately recovers topology, is robust to stochasticity, scales to thousand-node graphs, and outperforms baselines.
conclusion: The results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies electron trajectories in strong field ionization driven by squeezed light, focusing on the effect of quantum statistics on ultrafast electron dynamics.
motivation: To understand how squeezed light modifies electron dynamics in strong field ionization, beyond classical field descriptions.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte-Carlo technique to simulate ionization by squeezed states of light.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum distribution shows rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light offers experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics, but the atomic potential plays a crucial role.

title: Experimental Exclusion Of A Generalized Károlyházy Gravity-induced Decoherence Model
authors: Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola And Catalina Curceanu
abstract: We report new experimental constraints on the generalized version of the gravity-induced decoherence model originally proposed by Károlyházy. Using data collected by the VIP Collaboration at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory with a high-purity germanium detector, we derive an improved lower bound on the spatial correlation length characterizing metric fluctuations in the model. We obtain a bound m (95% C.L.), which exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the previous experimental limit. When combined with the theoretical upper bound m derived from macroscopic localization requirements, our result excludes the generalized Károlyházy model. The same conclusion applies to an associated non-Markovian formulation of the continuous spontaneous localization model. Our findings significantly tighten experimental constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios and demonstrate the sensitivity of underground low-background experiments to foundational modifications of quantum mechanics.
tldr: Experimental constraints exclude a gravity-induced decoherence model using underground detector data.
motivation: To test whether gravity causes wavefunction collapse via metric fluctuations, which would modify quantum mechanics.
method: Data from the VIP Collaboration's high-purity germanium detector at Gran Sasso were analyzed to bound the spatial correlation length of metric fluctuations.
result: A lower bound on the correlation length exceeding previous limits by an order of magnitude, combined with theoretical upper bounds, excludes the generalized Károlyházy model.
conclusion: The model is ruled out, tightening constraints on gravity-related decoherence and foundational quantum modifications.

title: A Maxwell Fish-eye Lens In A Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Jelte Duchêne, Elinor Kath, Floriane Arrouas, Hanyi Jang, Helmut Strobel, Markus K Oberthaler, Jay Mehta, Liam M Farrell, Wyatt Kirkby And Duncan H J O’dell
abstract: We experimentally realize an analogue of the optical Maxwell fish-eye lens (MFEL) using phononic excitations in a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC). A MFEL is characterized by a radially symmetric, spatially varying refractive index with the remarkable property that rays emitted from any point within the lens are perfectly focused at their antipodal points. While the implementation of such gradient-index lenses is challenging in conventional optical systems, BECs offer a highly tunable platform in which the spatially varying speed of sound of collective excitations—phonons, the acoustic analogues of photons—can be engineered and their dynamics observed in real time. Time-resolved measurements of phonon wavefronts reveal focusing behavior that shows good agreement with analytical theory and numerical simulations. This work provides both a geometric and physical framework for engineering effective refractive indices using ultracold atoms, and simulating wave propagation on effective spherical geometries.
tldr: This paper experimentally realizes an analogue of a Maxwell fish-eye lens using phononic excitations in a Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrating focusing of sound waves.
motivation: To create a highly tunable platform for simulating gradient-index lenses and wave propagation on curved geometries, which is challenging in conventional optics.
method: Phononic excitations in a BEC are used as acoustic analogues of photons; a spatially varying speed of sound is engineered to mimic the refractive index profile of a Maxwell fish-eye lens, and time-resolved imaging captures wavefront dynamics.
result: The phonon wavefronts exhibit focusing behavior consistent with analytical theory and numerical simulations, confirming the analogue.
conclusion: BECs provide a versatile platform for simulating wave propagation in effective curved spaces and gradient-index optics, with potential for studying analogues of gravitational systems.

title: Quantum Phases And Stability Of Bose–Hubbard Triangular Ladder With Magnetic Field
authors: Yue Jian, Jun-Hua Luo, Zi-Fa Yu, Juan Zhang, Ying-Ge Xu And Ju-Kui Xue
abstract: We investigate the ground state properties of interacting bosons on a triangular ladder subject to an artificial magnetic field. By means of the mean-field approximation, rich phases are revealed in the limit of weak interaction and large bosons occupation per site, including the Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, biased chiral superfluid (C-SF), C-SF and insulating phases. The quantum phases can be precisely identified and the underlying physics of phase transitions can be clarified by utilizing order parameters based on the atomic density, the effective rung current, and the current asymmetry ratio. Meanwhile, the phase transition of the system can be effectively controlled by adjusting the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux and the atomic interaction. Furthermore, using Bogoliubov theory, we have mapped the stability phase diagram across all parameters, and clarified the interdependence between superfluidity and the dispersion relation. The excitation spectrum, which effectively describes the system’s energetic stability, is governed by the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux, and the atomic interaction. Numerical simulations validate the dynamical instability of the system. This work offers a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases exhibited by ultracold atoms in optical lattices and new experimental approaches for achieving system superfluidity.
tldr: This paper studies ground state phases of bosons on a triangular ladder with a magnetic field using mean-field and Bogoliubov theory.
motivation: To explore quantum phases and stability in a bosonic ladder system under artificial magnetic fields.
method: Mean-field approximation and Bogoliubov theory are used to derive phase diagrams and excitation spectra.
result: Rich phases including Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, and chiral superfluid are identified, with stability mapped across parameters.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases in ultracold atoms in optical lattices.

title: Random-with-constraints: Constructing Minimal Models For High-dimensional Biology
authors: Ilya Nemenmanpankaj Mehtaahttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Physics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322bhttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Biology, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322chttps://ror.org/03czfpz43initiative In Theory And Modeling Of Living Systems, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322dhttps://ror.org/05qwgg493department Of Physics, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215ehttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing And Data Science, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
Biologists and physicists have a rich tradition of modeling dynamics of living systems with simple models composed of a few interacting components. Despite the remarkable success of this approach, it remains unclear how to use such finely tuned models to ...
tldr: This paper proposes a method for constructing minimal models of high-dimensional biological systems using random constraints.
motivation: Biologists and physicists often use simple models for complex living systems, but it is unclear how to systematically build such models from high-dimensional data.
method: The authors introduce a 'random-with-constraints' framework that generates minimal models by imposing random constraints that match observed statistics.
result: The approach yields interpretable models that capture essential dynamics while remaining tractable.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to construct minimal models for high-dimensional biological systems, bridging data-driven and theory-driven approaches.

title: Recursive Qlstm With Dynamic Variational Quantum Circuit Adaptation
authors: Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Yifeng Peng, Jiun-Cheng Jiang, Chun-Hua Lin, Kuo-Chung Peng, Junghoon Justin Park, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Hsin-Yi Lin, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Chen-Yu Liu, Shinjae Yoo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing and machine learning have motivated the development of quantum models for sequential data processing. In this paper, we propose a Recursive Quantum Long Short-Term Memory model, or Recursive QLSTM, which extends QLSTM through metacore-based recursive constructions. We numerically test the model under different input sequence lengths, metacore designs, and recursive rules, and identify the best-performing architecture among these variants. For this selected model, we further provide theoretical arguments explaining why its recursive structure improves temporal information propagation and enhances learning performance. Our results suggest that Recursive QLSTM offers a flexible and effective framework for quantum recurrent learning over input time series of various lengths.
tldr: Proposes a recursive quantum LSTM model for sequential data processing using dynamic variational quantum circuit adaptation.
motivation: To extend quantum machine learning to sequential data by improving temporal information propagation in QLSTM architectures.
method: Introduces metacore-based recursive constructions for QLSTM, tested on various input lengths and recursive rules, with theoretical analysis of the recursive structure.
result: Identifies best-performing architecture among variants; recursive structure improves learning performance on time series.
conclusion: Recursive QLSTM provides a flexible framework for quantum recurrent learning over variable-length sequences.

title: Leveraging Population Dynamics To Steer Efficient Search In Large-Scale Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Nikhat Khan, Ridge Redding, Nikhil Shukla
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems pose substantial computational challenges because their feasible solution spaces grow exponentially with problem size. This paper presents a GPU-accelerated augmented Population Annealing Monte Carlo (PAMC) framework for large-scale graph-partitioning problems, with emphasis on Max-Cut and Max-K-Cut. The proposed framework extends conventional PAMC by coupling population-based resampling with two stagnation-driven mechanisms: adaptive temperature control and energy-preserving nonlocal cluster moves. By using population-level optimization history as feedback, these mechanisms regulate the balance between exploration and refinement by reheating stalled populations and enabling collective transitions across locally confined regions of the solution space. Experiments on G-set benchmark instances show that the augmented PAMC framework achieves competitive or lower time-to-solution than reported state-of-the-art baselines on several large Max-Cut instances, while matching or improving solution quality under comparable runtime budgets. The solver also discovers a new best-known solution for the G63 Max-Cut instance and scales to a fully connected 100,000-spin Ising instance. For Max-3-Cut, the same framework establishes new best-known solutions on 36 G-set instances, demonstrating its applicability beyond binary Ising formulations. These results indicate that feedback-controlled population dynamics provide an effective and scalable strategy for steering stochastic search in large-scale combinatorial optimization.
tldr: A GPU-accelerated population annealing Monte Carlo framework for large-scale combinatorial optimization, applied to Max-Cut and Max-K-Cut problems.
motivation: Combinatorial optimization problems have exponentially growing solution spaces, requiring efficient algorithms for large instances.
method: Extends population annealing Monte Carlo with stagnation-driven adaptive temperature control and energy-preserving nonlocal cluster moves, implemented on GPU.
result: Achieves competitive or better time-to-solution on G-set benchmarks, discovers new best-known solutions for G63 Max-Cut and 36 Max-3-Cut instances, and scales to 100,000-spin Ising problems.
conclusion: Feedback-controlled population dynamics provide an effective and scalable strategy for stochastic search in large-scale combinatorial optimization.

title: Accelerating Chemical Potential Calculations With Minimal Normalizing Flows
authors: Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos Philippe Baron
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemical potentials are among the most important properties that can be obtained from a molecular simulation since they define many technologically relevant collective properties. The chemical potential of a species in solution is obtained by computing the free energy change of adding that species into a bulk system, a calculation typically very expensive for systems such as electrolytes, due to the lack of phase space overlap between "not-inserted" and "inserted" states. Recently, normalizing flows have been introduced as a way to accelerate free energy computations by learning a bijective function, constructed to be as expressive as possible, that maps the configuration space of one Boltzmann distribution onto another. This expressivity makes them difficult to train, limiting their ability to be generated "on-the-fly" for any new system, and in practice these mappings have shown only modest sampling improvements for liquids. We address these issues by introducing a "minimal" normalizing flow (MNF). This is a trainable bijective mapping that is intentionally limited in expressivity, and instead applies low-dimensional, physically informed transformations. Useful MNFs can be trained in 1 minute of GPU time due to their simplicity and our introduction of a novel training strategy. We show how calculations of chemical potentials of Lennard-Jones particle systems can be accelerated by at least 10 times with a simple radial mapping. We also apply a radial and orientational mapping to ion solvation in water, showing that MNFs can increase the effective sample size by 3 times for charging free energy calculations and 8 times for calculating free energy changes due to force field perturbations. This provides the foundation for the development of physically-informed mappings that can accelerate complex free energy calculations while retaining low training costs.
tldr: This paper introduces minimal normalizing flows to accelerate chemical potential calculations in molecular simulations, focusing on Lennard-Jones and electrolyte systems.
motivation: Chemical potential calculations via free energy methods are computationally expensive due to poor phase space overlap; normalizing flows can help but are often too complex to train efficiently.
method: The authors propose a minimal normalizing flow (MNF) with low-dimensional, physically informed transformations and a novel training strategy that enables training in about 1 minute on a GPU.
result: MNFs accelerate chemical potential calculations by 10x for Lennard-Jones systems and improve effective sample size by 3-8x for ion solvation in water.
conclusion: Physically informed, low-expressivity normalizing flows can significantly accelerate free energy calculations while keeping training costs low, providing a practical tool for molecular simulation.

title: Sums Of Squares In Polynomial Time
authors: Nikolas G\"artner, Victor Magron, Frank Vallentin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we analyze the bit complexity of deciding whether a given polynomial can be represented as a sum of squares of polynomials. We show that the weak membership problem for the sum-of-squares cone lies in [MATH]. Furthermore, we give a polynomial-time algorithm which computes, for a given polynomial and positive parameter [MATH], an [MATH]-relaxed closest sum-of-squares polynomial.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of sum-of-squares representations of polynomials, providing a polynomial-time algorithm for approximate sum-of-squares decomposition.
motivation: Determining whether a polynomial is a sum of squares is a fundamental problem in real algebraic geometry with applications in optimization, but its bit complexity was not well understood.
method: The authors analyze the weak membership problem for the sum-of-squares cone and develop an algorithm based on semidefinite programming and rounding techniques.
result: They show that the weak membership problem lies in the complexity class NP and give a polynomial-time algorithm that computes an epsilon-relaxed closest sum-of-squares polynomial.
conclusion: The work establishes the polynomial-time solvability of approximate sum-of-squares decomposition, advancing the theoretical understanding of this problem.

title: Laplace--Fisher Gate Identities For Optimal Matrix-Gated Blended Score Estimation
authors: Tan Bui Tanh Alois Duston
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling from an unnormalized target by reversing an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion requires the score of each noise-perturbed marginal. Tweedie's identity and a target-score identity give unbiased finite-reference estimators for this score. Scalar blends can reduce variance, but are too rigid for singular or strongly anisotropic targets. We cast blended score estimation as conditional risk minimization over matrix-valued blending coefficients, or gates, and derive the variance-optimal gate [ \Gstar(y,t)=\alphat^2\bigl(\alphat^2 I_d+\gammat,\E[H_0(X_0)\mid Y_t=y]\bigr)^{-1},\qquad H_0=-\nabla^2\log p_0 . ] Here (\alphat=e^{-t}) and (\gammat=1-e^{-2t}). We call this formula the (\LFGI{}). Since the Tweedie--TSI disagreement has conditional mean zero, the gate changes estimator variance without changing its expected value. We give the Gaussian special case and prove finite-reference consistency and stability bounds for estimating the gate from weighted reference samples. We apply the finite-reference LFGI estimator to normalized density evaluation for Bayesian inverse problems. When MCMC pilot samples and derivative information are available, LFGI uses these byproducts to construct a normalized posterior-density surrogate. The surrogate enables posterior-energy evaluation, model-evidence estimation, and density-based diagnostics beyond those available from samples alone. On a PDE-constrained inverse-problem benchmark, LFGI improves posterior-density calibration and sampling diagnostics relative to the other tested score-estimator classes, and known-evidence experiments check absolute calibration in Gaussian and non-Gaussian settings.
tldr: This paper introduces a matrix-valued blending technique for score estimation in diffusion models, applied to Bayesian inverse problems.
motivation: Existing scalar blending for score estimation is too rigid for singular or anisotropic targets, motivating a more flexible matrix-valued approach.
method: The authors derive the variance-optimal matrix gate via conditional risk minimization, using Tweedie's identity and a target-score identity, and prove finite-sample consistency.
result: The Laplace-Fisher Gate Identity provides the optimal blending matrix, and the estimator improves posterior-density calibration and sampling diagnostics on a PDE-constrained inverse problem.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a principled way to reduce variance in score estimation, with practical benefits for normalized density evaluation in Bayesian inverse problems.

title: Closed-form Solutions To Some Generalized Variational Inference Problems
authors: Jacob Westerhout Hien Duy Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Donsker--Varadhan formula characterizes the ordinary Bayesian posterior as the solution of an unrestricted [MATH]-regularized variational problem. Generalized variational inference replaces this regularizer by other divergences, but the resulting measure-valued optimization problem is often studied only after restriction to a parametric variational family. This paper studies the unrestricted measure-level problem. Given a measurable space [MATH], a prior probability measure [MATH], a measurable loss [MATH], a regularization strength [MATH], and a divergence [MATH], we seek probability measures in \[ ()}{}\left\{\int_{} \ell\,Q+\alpha(Q\Vert P)\right\}. \] For [MATH]-divergence penalties we derive a scalar inverse-gradient density formula and a one-dimensional dual identity; the Kullback--Leibler, Cressie--Read, and squared-Hellinger problems are treated as examples. Reverse [MATH]-divergences and mixed forward/reverse Kullback--Leibler penalties follow from the same separable integral principle. For Bregman divergences between densities we obtain a density-space solution with a scalar mass multiplier, including least-squares, density-power, and Burg/Itakura--Saito examples. For R\'enyi penalties of order [MATH] we derive a normalized truncated-power characterization and a threshold equation for every global optimizer. Finite model-weight formulas and simple conjugate Bayesian model illustrations show how these closed forms are realized in practice and differ from the traditional solutions.
tldr: This paper derives closed-form solutions for generalized variational inference problems using various divergences, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Generalized variational inference replaces the Kullback-Leibler divergence with other divergences, but unrestricted measure-level solutions are rarely studied.
method: The authors derive closed-form density formulas for f-divergences, reverse f-divergences, Bregman divergences, and Rényi penalties using scalar inverse-gradient and threshold equations.
result: Closed-form solutions are obtained for several divergence families, including Kullback-Leibler, Cressie-Read, squared-Hellinger, least-squares, density-power, and Burg/Itakura-Saito divergences.
conclusion: The closed forms enable practical implementation and differ from traditional Bayesian posteriors, but the work is purely in statistical inference and machine learning.

title: Interplay Between VAoI, Packet Error Rate, And Delay For Energy-Efficient Remote Monitoring
authors: Yasaman Khorsandmanesh, Zinat Behdad, Emil Bjornson, Cicek Cavdar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter studies energy optimization of short-packet transmission for event-triggered remote monitoring over finite-blocklength wireless links. A wireless sensor node generates updates only when the source state changes, and freshness is measured by the Version Age of Information (VAoI). We model the VAoI evolution as a Markov chain and show its coupling with the packet error rate, characterized by decoding error probability, and average delay. Then, we formulate a transmit-power allocation problem that minimizes the long-term average energy consumption under a VAoI constraint and solve it using a low-complexity search method. Numerical results show that the update arrival probability and blocklength strongly affect the energy--VAoI tradeoff, and that optimizing long-term energy consumption can substantially reduce energy compared with minimizing the energy per transmission.
tldr: This paper optimizes energy consumption for event-triggered remote monitoring using Version Age of Information (VAoI) over finite-blocklength wireless links.
motivation: To minimize energy consumption in wireless sensor networks while maintaining freshness of information measured by VAoI.
method: Models VAoI evolution as a Markov chain coupled with packet error rate and delay, then formulates a transmit-power allocation problem solved via low-complexity search.
result: Update arrival probability and blocklength significantly affect the energy-VAoI tradeoff; optimizing long-term energy consumption reduces energy compared to per-transmission optimization.
conclusion: Energy-efficient remote monitoring can be achieved by jointly considering VAoI, packet error rate, and delay in short-packet transmission.

title: Zero-Threshold Discrepancies For Multiple Correlation Sequences
authors: Kangbo Ouyang, Jiahao Qiu, Xiangdong Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the zero-threshold lifting problem for polynomial multiple correlation sequences with respect to the measure-theoretic pro-nilfactor. The structure theory for polynomial multiple averages implies that, at every positive threshold, positivity on the pro-nilfactor lifts to positivity in the original system, except on a set of zero upper Banach density. We demonstrate that this lifting property does not hold at the zero threshold. Specifically, we construct an ergodic system and two sets of positive measure for which the pro-nilfactor correlation is positive along a set of times with positive upper density, while the corresponding exact correlation vanishes on this set. This provides a negative answer to a question posed by Glasscock, Koutsogiannis, Le, Moreira, Richter, and Robertson. %. Additionally, we prove a corresponding rigidity property. For any ergodic system, any essentially distinct family of integer polynomials vanishing at the origin, and any tuple of non-negative bounded functions, the zero-threshold discrepancy set is not piecewise syndetic.
tldr: This paper studies zero-threshold discrepancies for polynomial multiple correlation sequences in ergodic theory, showing that a lifting property fails at zero threshold.
motivation: To answer a question by Glasscock et al. about whether positivity on the pro-nilfactor lifts to positivity in the original system at zero threshold.
method: Constructs an explicit ergodic system and two sets of positive measure, then analyzes correlations using measure-theoretic pro-nilfactor and polynomial multiple averages.
result: The lifting property does not hold at zero threshold; the pro-nilfactor correlation can be positive on a set of positive upper density while the exact correlation vanishes there.
conclusion: The zero-threshold discrepancy set is not piecewise syndetic, providing a negative answer to the posed question.

title: Communication Complexity Of Point-line Incidences Over The Reals
authors: Hamed Hatami Marcel K. Goh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a point-line incidence problem over the reals whose randomized communication complexity is constant, but whose deterministic communication complexity is linear even when the players have access to an equality oracle. This is the strongest possible separation between these two measures, and it improves on an earlier [MATH]-versus-[MATH] separation of G\"o\"os, Harms, and Riazanov. Because point-line incidence problems have constant sign rank, our construction also bears on a question of Harms and Zamaraev, who asked whether constant sign rank together with constant randomized communication complexity forces constant equality-oracle complexity. This was already refuted by G\"o\"os, Harms, Imbach, and Sokolov with a logarithmic lower bound; our example improves the separation to linear, which is optimal. The proof draws on a construction in the recent disproof of the sum-product conjecture over the reals by Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut, and Zhelezov, using totally real number fields of large degree and small discriminant.
tldr: This paper proves a linear separation between deterministic and randomized communication complexity for point-line incidence problems over the reals, using number-theoretic constructions.
motivation: To understand the power of randomness in communication complexity and to answer questions about sign rank and equality-oracle complexity.
method: Constructs a point-line incidence problem based on totally real number fields of large degree and small discriminant, inspired by a recent disproof of the sum-product conjecture.
result: Achieves constant randomized communication complexity but linear deterministic complexity even with an equality oracle, which is optimal.
conclusion: The separation is the strongest possible, refuting a conjecture that constant sign rank and constant randomized complexity force constant equality-oracle complexity.

title: General Techniques For Reducing Key-Switching Overhead In Privacy-Preserving Two-Party Transformer Inference
authors: Wenshao Yang, Zhenhua Liu, Dongdong Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In secure two-party Transformer inference, linear layers are typically evaluated using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) through plaintext-ciphertext or ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications, where key switching primarily occurs and dominates computational overhead in both FHE-based and hybrid FHE-MPC systems. Existing optimizations rely heavily on packing-specific algorithms, limiting their general applicability. Targeting this overhead from a packing-independent perspective, we propose a preprocessing-assisted method for secure attention computation. By decomposing attention into precomputable operations and online interactions, this method reduces online inference-phase key switching without modifying existing packing strategies. However, the first method shifting key switching offline introduces additional storage requirements. To address this, we propose storage-communication trade-off techniques that replace large precomputed ciphertexts with modest online communication, enabling flexible deployment under varying resource constraints. While ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplication is offloaded to the preprocessing phase in hybrid schemes and the first layer of FHE-based schemes, these operations still persist in the offline stage and subsequent FHE layers. To further optimize it, we propose a fused key-switch technique targeting the multiplication-followed-by-rotation pattern, which frequently arises in existing RNS-CKKS matrix multiplication schemes. By combining relinearization and rotation into a single procedure, this technique reduces the associated computation costs. Analytical evaluations demonstrate that our proposed techniques significantly reduce online key-switch overhead and provide flexible trade-offs between storage and communication without requiring modifications to existing packing strategies.
tldr: This paper proposes techniques to reduce key-switching overhead in secure two-party Transformer inference using FHE, focusing on packing-independent optimizations.
motivation: Key-switching dominates computational overhead in FHE-based and hybrid FHE-MPC systems for secure Transformer inference, and existing optimizations are packing-specific.
method: The authors propose a preprocessing-assisted method for secure attention computation, a storage-communication trade-off technique, and a fused key-switch technique for multiplication-followed-by-rotation patterns.
result: Analytical evaluations show significant reduction in online key-switch overhead and flexible trade-offs between storage and communication without modifying packing strategies.
conclusion: The proposed techniques effectively reduce key-switching overhead in privacy-preserving Transformer inference, offering general applicability across different packing schemes.

title: MAP-Based Task-Oriented Precoding For Multiuser Communication
authors: Mohammad Javad Ahmadi, Rafael F. Schaefer, H. Vincent Poor
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a task-oriented multiuser wireless communication framework for distributed classification based on a MAP-driven system design under wireless channel impairments. By deriving a tractable class-mean separation objective, the proposed approach enables low-complexity design of both learning-based feature extraction and precoding strategies. Unlike existing covariance-based and reconstruction-oriented methods, the proposed formulation avoids repeated covariance inversions and eigen-decomposition operations while directly improving class separability after channel distortion. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher classification accuracy than existing schemes, while simultaneously reducing computational complexity.
tldr: A task-oriented precoding framework for multiuser wireless communication using MAP-based optimization to improve classification accuracy.
motivation: Existing precoding methods for multiuser communication are not optimized for task-oriented objectives like classification, leading to suboptimal performance under channel impairments.
method: Derives a tractable class-mean separation objective to jointly design feature extraction and precoding, avoiding covariance inversions and eigen-decompositions.
result: Achieves higher classification accuracy and lower computational complexity compared to covariance-based and reconstruction-oriented methods.
conclusion: The proposed MAP-based approach is effective for task-oriented communication in wireless systems with channel distortions.

title: On The Encodability Of Reversible Process Calculi
authors: Ivan Lanese, Claudio Antares Mezzina, Iain Phillips, Irek Ulidowski, Shoji Yuen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reversibility, allowing one to execute a program not only forwards as usual, but also backwards, has emerged as a main concept in computing, with applications ranging from debugging and fault tolerance to biological and quantum systems. CCSK, a reversible extension of CCS, is a paradigmatic model of reversible concurrent computation. In this paper, we investigate the encodability of CCSK into classical forward-only concurrent models. We establish a separation theorem showing that there is no basic, success-sensitive encoding of CCSK into CCS or the {\pi}-calculus, highlighting the strong impact of reversibility on the expressive power. We then present an encoding of CCSK processes with only top-level parallel composition into the internal {\pi}-calculus, correct up to strong bisimilarity. We also identify a fundamental limitation: no parallel-preserving encoding of CCSK (with arbitrary parallel composition) into the {\pi}-calculus can be correct up to strong bisimilarity. Finally, we provide a parallel-preserving encoding correct under a weaker behavioural correspondence: weak mutual simulation. Our findings extend the literature of encodability results to reversible process calculi.
tldr: This paper studies the encodability of reversible process calculi (CCSK) into forward-only models like CCS and π-calculus, establishing separation and encoding results.
motivation: Reversibility is important for debugging, fault tolerance, and quantum systems, but its impact on expressive power in concurrent computation is not well understood.
method: The authors prove impossibility results via separation theorems and construct explicit encodings with correctness up to strong bisimilarity or weak mutual simulation.
result: No basic, success-sensitive encoding of CCSK into CCS or π-calculus exists; parallel-preserving encoding is impossible for strong bisimilarity but possible for weak mutual simulation.
conclusion: Reversibility fundamentally increases expressive power, and encoding reversible processes requires weaker behavioral equivalences.

method: Experimental and theoretical analysis of the folding/unfolding dynamics of Trichoplax adhaerens, linking crease geometry to cilia motion.
result: Creases act as information bottlenecks that regulate the collective motion of cilia, creating a feedback loop.
conclusion: The study reveals a new mechanism for information processing in biological active matter, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
